title: MemPoison: Uncovering Persistent Memory Threats and Structural Blind Spots in LLM Agents
claim: Poisoned memories evade write-time defenses through increasingly subtle attack tiers, and all models show substantial corruption that rises with difficulty.
layout: 2 parts: three side-by-side flow panels left, radar chart right; top-to-bottom flows
description: The left part of the figure has three gray rounded panels labeled L1 Single Record Corruption, L2 Compositional Corruption, and L3 Context-Triggered Dormant Corruption. Each panel runs top to bottom. An attacker icon writes poisoned memory records, shown as red documents with skull marks. The records pass a green-shield write-time defense, then enter a blue persistent memory store holding gray benign documents and red poisoned ones. A user query then reaches an agent robot, which ends in a green Safe Action box or a red Unsafe Action box. L1 shows a blocked record. L2 shows several individually benign records combining into one unsafe retrieval. L3 adds a clock-marked record and a context trigger. The right part is a radar chart of behavioral corruption rate for ten named models, with three colored lines for L1, L2 and L3. L3 is the largest, in teal. The panels carry captions (a) and (b).
caption: The left panel illustrates how poisoned memories pass through write-time admission, persistent storage, retrieval, and trigger-time use across L1--L3. The right panel reports behavioral corruption rate under NONE, showing substantial cross agent vulnerability along the difficulty ladder.
abstract: Persistent external memory enhances agent continuity but introduces persistent security vulnerabilities: adversarial content can be injected via standard interaction channels, retained across turns, and later distort downstream behavior. To address this challenge, we propose MemPoison, a comprehensive benchmark and analysis framework featuring 1227 hand-validated cases across four attack types, three injection channels, and three representative memory substrates, evaluated on seven open-weight and three closed-weight model families. We introduce a three-tier taxonomy: (L1) direct single-record corruption, (L2) compositional multi-record corruption and (L3) context-triggered dormant corruption. Our evaluations reveal a distinct defense frontier: while baseline write-time defenses, such as consistency checks, substantially suppress direct L1 attacks, they fail to reliably suppress L2 and L3 attacks. Through mechanistic influence decomposition (MID), we demonstrate structural blind spots in write-time defenses, which admit seemingly benign records that later become harmful through joint retrieval composition or trigger-conditioned activation. Our findings advocate for shifting from static filtering to adaptive, context-sensitive memory defense strategies.
